main/grammar-and-syntax.html.title: Grammar and Syntax
main/grammar-and-syntax.html.description:
Syntax refers to the rules that determine how symbols/tokens can be arranged to form valid programs or statements.
Uses: Alphabet — the set of allowed symbols.
Lexicon — the collection of valid words/tokens.
Sequences of symbols or tokens — arranged according to syntactic rules. Defines the rules for creating acceptable grammar/structures in a language.
A Context-Free Grammar (CFG) is a formal system used to describe the syntax of programming languages.
Syntax trees (parse trees) represent the hierarchical structure of a program or expression. They show how operations and components are organized according to the grammar.
The hierarchy of operations can be represented visually through the tree. Grammar is a set of rules that defines how valid statements or expressions can be formed in a language.
In programming languages, grammar determines whether a sequence of tokens is syntactically valid.
CFG is commonly used to formally describe programming-language grammar. Interpretation The program is executed statement by statement, sequentially, by an interpreter.
The interpreter translates/executes instructions as the program runs. Compilation The program is translated before execution into another form, such as machine code or intermediate code.
The resulting code can then be executed. Linker Combines separately compiled pieces of machine/object code into a single executable program.
It can also resolve references between separately compiled modules or libraries before execution. Java Translation Java uses compiler to translate source into bytecode
Then uses Java Virtual Machine (JVM) to interpret bytecode (execution) Since bytecode is low-level and easy to interpret, JVM is small Translation flow:
Source Code → Compiler → Bytecode → JVM → Hardware Source code — program written by the programmer.
Compiler — translates source code into intermediate code.
Intermediate code — platform-independent representation.
Virtual machine — executes the intermediate code.
Simulator/Hardware — ultimately carries out the operations.

Modules help organize a program by dividing code into smaller, reusable structures. Two common types are procedures and functions.A procedure is a named block of code that performs a specific task. Organizes monolithic code into smaller, manageable structures. Improves readability, maintainability, and code reuse. Generally does not return a value directly. May accept parameters and may modify values through output/reference parameters. Does not fundamentally change the overall process flow; it encapsulates a set of operations. CALL procedureName(arguments) A function is a reusable block of code that accepts input and returns a value. Derived from the mathematical concept of a function: input → output. Accepts input through parameters. Performs a computation or operation. Returns a value to the caller. Can be used as part of an expression. SET variableName = functionName(arguments) A lambda function is an anonymous function—a function defined without explicitly giving it a name. It is useful for creating small functions on the fly, especially when a function is needed only temporarily or as an argument to another function.lambda x: x * 2 This represents a function that: accepts x as its parameter returns x * 2 Anonymous — normally does not have an explicit function name. Single-expression — typically contains one expression whose value is returned. First-class — can be assigned to Variables, passed as arguments, and returned from other functions. Lightweight — convenient for short, simple operations. FUNCTION square(x) RETURN x * x END FUNCTION Equivalent lambda-style expression:lambda x: x * x A lambda is best suited for short, simple operations. For complex logic, a regular named function is generally clearer.seealso

main/parameters-and-arguments.html.description:
Parameters are Variables defined in the method/function/procedure declaration.
Arguments are the actual values supplied when calling the method/function/procedure.FUNCTION add(a, b) ← a and b are parameters SET result = add(5, 3) ← 5 and 3 are arguments
Method parameters are also called local parameters because they are available within the scope of the method.Parameters can be passed in different ways depending on the programming language or system.A value parameter receives a copy of the value supplied by the caller. The procedure/function can use the value.
Changes made to the parameter generally do not change the caller's original variable.
A reference parameter provides access to the caller's variable or object reference.
Changes made through the parameter can affect the original variable. Useful when a procedure needs to modify a value supplied by the caller. IN JAVA There is no pass-by-reference It still uses pass-by-value but instead we pass the address of the object as the value These parameter modes are commonly used in stored procedures, particularly in SQL/database systems.An IN parameter passes a value into the procedure. Used as input. Can be used in SQL statements and calculations. The procedure does not use it to return a modified value to the caller. CALL procedureName(inputValue) Direction: Caller → ProcedureAn OUT parameter passes a value out of the procedure. Used to return a result from the procedure. The procedure assigns or modifies the parameter. The resulting value can be retrieved by the caller after the procedure executes. Direction: Procedure → Caller An OUT parameter is not necessarily returned as a result set; it is a separate output value. A stored procedure can also return a result set independently. An INOUT parameter combines the behavior of IN and OUT parameters. Receives an initial value from the caller. The procedure can modify that value. The modified value is passed back to the caller. Direction: Caller → Procedure → Caller*The procedure may be able to assign to its local copy depending on the language, but the change is not returned through the parameter.

main/scoping.html.title: Scoping
main/scoping.html.description:
Scope determines where a variable can be accessed or used in a program.
The major variable scopes in Java are:
Variables declared inside a Class but outside any method, constructor, or block. These are usually called fields.
If declared with static, they are Class Variables.
Can be accessed by methods in the Class, depending on their access modifier.
static Variables can be accessed through the Class itself. class Example { static int count = 10; // class variable }
Note: Java does not technically have "global Variables" like some other programming languages. What are often called global Variables are usually Class/static Variables.
Variables declared inside a Class but outside methods, without static.
Each object gets its own copy of the variable.
Also called instance Variables. They can be accessed through an object. class Student { String name; // instance variable int age; // instance variable } Each Student object can have a different name and age.
Variables declared inside a method, constructor, or function-like block. They can only be accessed within the area where they are declared.
They are created when the method/block starts executing and are no longer accessible after it ends. void greet() { String message = "Hello"; // local variable System.out.println(message); } message cannot be accessed outside greet().
Parameters are Variables passed into a method or constructor.
They are only available inside that method or constructor. void greet(String name) { System.out.println("Hello " + name); } Here, name is a parameter and can only be used inside greet(). A block is a section of code enclosed in curly braces {}.
Variables declared inside a block can only be used within that block. Common examples include: if statements for loops while loops switch statements if (true) { int x = 10; System.out.println(x); } // x cannot be accessed here
A variable declared inside the if block is not accessible outside it.
In Java, Variables declared inside a method are local to that method.void first() { int x = 10; } void second() { // x cannot be accessed here }
The variable x belongs only to first().
Java does not have function scope in exactly the same terminology as JavaScript, but method-local Variables have a similar idea: they are accessible only within their method/block.
Hoisting refers to the behavior where variable or function declarations are treated as if they are moved to the top of their scope before execution.
Java does not have JavaScript-style variable hoisting.For example:public class Example { public static void main(String[] args) { System.out.println(x); // Error int x = 10; } } This produces an error because x must be declared before it is used.
JavaScript JavaScript has hoisting behavior, but it depends on how the variable is declared: var → declaration is hoisted. let and const → declarations are hoisted internally but cannot be accessed before declaration because of the Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ). Function declarations can generally be called before their declaration.

main/variables.html.description:
A variable is a named storage location used to hold a value that can change during program execution. note on initialization: Class variables are implicitly initialized A primitive variable stores a primitive value. Java has eight primitive data types: Example:int age = 20; double price = 19.99; char grade = 'A'; boolean active = true; Conceptually, a primitive variable contains its value directly.age ┌───────┐ │ 20 │ └───────┘ The exact physical memory representation is managed by the JVM and should not be treated as a Java-level memory address.
seealso Casting & Conversion on Assignment
Scoping A reference variable holds a reference to an object rather than the object itself. Example:String name = "Alice"; Conceptually:name │ ▼ ┌─────────────┐ │ "Alice" │ │ Object │ └─────────────┘ A reference is often described as being pointer-like, but Java does not provide direct pointer manipulation like C or C++. Classes Interfaces Arrays Enums String

main/bigdecimal.html.title: BigDecimal
main/bigdecimal.html.description: Class for arbitrary-precision decimal numbers Used when exact decimal calculations are important Commonly used for money, financial calculations, and precise measurements Immutable Cannot use arithmetic operators like +, -, *, / BigDecimal price = new BigDecimal("19.99"); BigDecimal tax = new BigDecimal("1.50"); BigDecimal total = price.add(tax); BigDecimal value = new BigDecimal("0.1"); Prefer the String constructor for decimal values Preserves the exact decimal value provided Warning Never pass a raw double literal to the constructor. double uses binary floating-point representation Values such as 0.1 cannot be represented exactly as a double The resulting BigDecimal can therefore contain floating-point inaccuracies new BigDecimal("0.1"); // Exactly 0.1 new BigDecimal(0.1); // Inaccurate representation add() → adds two values subtract() → subtracts two values multiply() → multiplies two values divide() → divides two values remainder() → returns the remainder compareTo() → compares two values setScale() → changes the decimal scale abs() → returns the absolute value Always define the scale and rounding mode when division may produce a non-terminating decimal Prevents ArithmeticException Use RoundingMode to specify how the result should be rounded BigDecimal result = new BigDecimal("10").divide(new BigDecimal("3"), 2, RoundingMode.HALF_UP); System.out.println(result); // 3.33 Use compareTo() for numerical comparison equals() also considers the scale BigDecimal a = new BigDecimal("10.0"); BigDecimal b = new BigDecimal("10.00"); a.compareTo(b); // 0 a.equals(b); // false

main/biginteger.html.title: BigInteger
main/biginteger.html.description:
Class for arbitrary-precision integer numbers Used when integers can exceed the range of primitive types like long Commonly used for cryptography, large calculations, and exact integer arithmetic Immutable Cannot use arithmetic operators like +, -, *, / BigInteger a = new BigInteger("100000000000000000000"); BigInteger b = new BigInteger("200000000000000000000"); BigInteger sum = a.add(b); BigInteger value = new BigInteger("12345678901234567890"); String constructor is useful for large integer values No precision is lost because the value is stored as an exact integer BigInteger value = BigInteger.valueOf(1000L); valueOf() is convenient for primitive integer values add() → adds two values subtract() → subtracts two values multiply() → multiplies two values divide() → performs integer division remainder() → returns the remainder mod() → returns the non-negative remainder pow() → raises the value to an integer power gcd() → returns the greatest common divisor abs() → returns the absolute value negate() → returns the negative value compareTo() → compares two values max() → returns the larger value min() → returns the smaller value divide() performs integer division Any fractional part is discarded BigInteger a = new BigInteger("10"); BigInteger b = new BigInteger("3"); BigInteger result = a.divide(b); System.out.println(result); // 3
Note Unlike BigDecimal, BigInteger does not use scale or rounding because it represents integers only. Use compareTo() for numerical comparison equals() checks whether two BigInteger objects have the same value BigInteger a = new BigInteger("100"); BigInteger b = new BigInteger("100"); a.compareTo(b); // 0 a.equals(b); // true

main/calendar.html.title: Calendar
main/calendar.html.description:
Abstract Class used to work with dates and times Located in java.util Provides methods for manipulating individual date/time fields such as year, month, day, hour, and minute
More flexible than Date for date/time manipulation Considered part of the legacy date/time API Calendar calendar = Calendar.getInstance(); System.out.println(calendar.get(Calendar.YEAR)); get(field) → returns the value of a specific date/time field set(field, value) → changes a specific date/time field add(field, amount) → adds or subtracts an amount from a field roll(field, amount) → changes a field without affecting larger fields getTime() → converts the Calendar into a Date setTime(date) → sets the calendar using a Date getTimeInMillis() → returns the time as milliseconds since the Unix epoch setTimeInMillis(milliseconds) → sets the calendar using milliseconds before(calendar) → checks if this calendar occurs before another after(calendar) → checks if this calendar occurs after another Calendar fields are accessed using constants:Calendar.YEAR Calendar.MONTH Calendar.DAY_OF_MONTH Calendar.HOUR Calendar.MINUTE Calendar.SECOND Example:Calendar calendar = Calendar.getInstance(); int year = calendar.get(Calendar.YEAR); int month = calendar.get(Calendar.MONTH); int day = calendar.get(Calendar.DAY_OF_MONTH); Month starts at 0 Calendar.MONTH is zero-based: 0 → January 1 → February 11 → December Calendar calendar = Calendar.getInstance(); getInstance() → returns a Calendar configured for the default locale and time zone A specific time zone can also be used:Calendar calendar = Calendar.getInstance(TimeZone.getTimeZone("UTC"));

main/date.html.title: Date
main/date.html.description:
Class representing a specific date and time Located in java.util Stores time internally as the number of milliseconds since January 1, 1970, 00:00:00 UTC Mutable Considered a legacy date/time API
Modern Java code generally prefers java.time classes such as LocalDate, LocalDateTime, and Instant Date date = new Date(); System.out.println(date); new Date() → creates a Date representing the current date and time getTime() → returns the time as milliseconds since the Unix epoch setTime(milliseconds) → changes the date/time using milliseconds since the epoch before(date) → checks if this date occurs before another date after(date) → checks if this date occurs after another date equals(date) → checks if two dates represent the same point in time compareTo(date) → compares two dates chronologically Date now = new Date(); Date date = new Date(0); new Date() → current date and time new Date(0) → January 1, 1970, 00:00:00 UTC Using milliseconds:long millis = System.currentTimeMillis(); Date date = new Date(millis); Date first = new Date(); Date second = new Date(); if (first.before(second)) { System.out.println("First comes before second"); } before() / after() are useful for chronological comparisons compareTo() returns: negative → this date comes before the other 0 → dates represent the same time positive → this date comes after the other Date itself does not provide modern formatting functionality. Use SimpleDateFormat for legacy code:SimpleDateFormat format = new SimpleDateFormat("yyyy-MM-dd"); String result = format.format(new Date());
For modern Java, prefer java.time and DateTimeFormatter.

main/dateformat.html.title: DateFormat
main/dateformat.html.description:

Note For custom date patterns, use SimpleDateFormat. For new applications, prefer java.time classes such as LocalDate, LocalDateTime, and ZonedDateTime.

main/duration.html.title: Duration
main/duration.html.description:
Class representing an amount of time Stores time-based amounts in seconds and nanoseconds Commonly used with LocalTime, LocalDateTime, Instant, and other time-based classes
Immutable and Thread Safe Part of the modern Java date/time API Duration duration = Duration.ofHours(2); ofDays(days) → creates a duration in days ofHours(hours) → creates a duration in hours ofMinutes(minutes) → creates a duration in minutes ofSeconds(seconds) → creates a duration in seconds ofMillis(milliseconds) → creates a duration in milliseconds ofNanos(nanoseconds) → creates a duration in nanoseconds between(start, end) → calculates the duration between two temporal values parse(text) → creates a duration from an ISO-8601 string Duration duration = Duration.ofHours(2); Duration duration = Duration.ofMinutes(30); getSeconds() → returns the number of seconds getNano() → returns the nanosecond adjustment toDays() → converts the duration to days toHours() → converts the duration to hours toMinutes() → converts the duration to minutes toSeconds() → converts the duration to seconds toMillis() → converts the duration to milliseconds isZero() → checks if the duration is zero isNegative() → checks if the duration is negative Duration is immutable, so modification methods return a new Duration.Duration duration = Duration.ofHours(2); Duration longer = duration.plusMinutes(30); Duration shorter = duration.minusMinutes(15); plus() / minus() → adds or subtracts a duration plusHours() / minusHours() → adds/subtracts hours plusMinutes() / minusMinutes() → adds/subtracts minutes plusSeconds() / minusSeconds() → adds/subtracts seconds multipliedBy() → multiplies the duration dividedBy() → divides the duration negated() → returns the negative duration LocalTime start = LocalTime.of(9, 0); LocalTime end = LocalTime.of(17, 30); Duration duration = Duration.between(start, end); duration.toHours(); // 8 duration.toMinutes(); // 510 Period → date-based: years, months, days Duration → time-based: hours, minutes, seconds, nanoseconds

main/file.html.title: File
main/file.html.description:
Class representing a file or directory path
Used to inspect and manipulate files/directories
Does not read or write file contents
Can represent a path that does not exist
File file = new File("data.txt");
File dir = new File("documents"); Path can be relative or absolute exists() → checks if the file/directory exists

main/fileinputstream.html.title: FileInputStream
main/fileinputstream.html.description:
Class used to read raw bytes from a file
Useful for reading binary data such as images, PDFs, and other files
Can also read text when bytes are converted into characters
FileInputStream in = new FileInputStream("data.txt"); Opens the file for reading
Throws FileNotFoundException if the file doesn't exist read() → reads one byte; returns -1 when the end is reached
read(byte[]) → reads bytes into an array
read(byte[], offset, length) → reads part of an array
available() → returns estimated bytes available to read
skip() → skips bytes
close() → closes the stream

write(byte[]) → writes an entire byte array
write(byte[], offset, length) → writes part of a byte array
flush() → forces buffered data to be written

try (FileOutputStream out = new FileOutputStream("data.txt")) { byte[] data = "Hello".getBytes(Charset.forName("utf8")); out.write(data);
}

FileReader reader = new FileReader("data.txt", Charset.forName("utf8")); Opens the file for reading
Throws FileNotFoundException if the file doesn't exist read() → reads one character; returns -1 at the end
read(char[]) → reads characters into an array
read(char[], offset, length) → reads part of an array
skip() → skips characters
ready() → checks if the reader is ready to be read

main/filewriter.html.description:
Class used to write character data to a file
Designed for text files
Reads per character

write(char[]) → writes a character array
write(String) → writes a string

main/instant.html.title: Instant
main/instant.html.description:
Class representing an instantaneous point on the timeline Represents time relative to UTC Useful for timestamps, logging, event tracking, and measuring elapsed time Not tied to a specific time zone Immutable and thread-safe
Can be converted to ZonedDateTime Instant now = Instant.now(); Returns the current moment in UTC Instant epoch = Instant.EPOCH; Represents 1970-01-01T00:00:00Z Instant instant = Instant.ofEpochSecond(0); 0 seconds = Unix epoch Instant instant = Instant.ofEpochMilli(1000); 1000 milliseconds = 1 second after the epoch now() → returns the current instant ofEpochSecond() → creates an instant from epoch seconds ofEpochMilli() → creates an instant from epoch milliseconds getEpochSecond() → returns seconds since the Unix epoch toEpochMilli() → returns milliseconds since the Unix epoch plusSeconds() → adds seconds plusMillis() → adds milliseconds minusSeconds() → subtracts seconds isBefore() → checks if this instant occurs before another isAfter() → checks if this instant occurs after another equals() → checks if two instants represent the same moment Instant start = Instant.now(); // some operation Instant end = Instant.now(); if (end.isAfter(start)) { System.out.println("Finished later"); } Instant instant = Instant.now(); ZonedDateTime dateTime = instant.atZone( ZoneId.of("Asia/Manila") ); The instant stays the same
The displayed date/time changes according to the ZoneID Instant.now() 2026-09-09T02:00:00Z ↓ atZone() ZoneId: Asia/Manila ↓ 2026-09-09T10:00:00+08:00
Instant can be extracted from java.util.Date and java.util.Calendar.
Useful for converting from old Date and Calendar to ZonedDateTime or other java.time objects.
See also ZoneID. // convert from Calendar to LocalDateTime Calendar calendar = Calendar.getInstance(); LocalDateTime calendarLocalDate = LocalDateTime.ofInstant(calendar.toInstant(), ZoneId.of("Asia/Manila")); // convert from Date to LocalDateTime Date now = new Date() LocalDateTime calendarLocalDate = LocalDateTime.ofInstant(now.toInstant(), ZoneId.of("Asia/Manila"));

main/iterables.html.title: Iterables
main/iterables.html.description:
Interface representing something that can be iterated over Provides a standard way to traverse elements one at a time
Implemented by most Java collections Allows an object to be used with the enhanced for loop for (String name : names) { System.out.println(name); }
iterator() → returns an Iterator for traversing elements forEach() → performs an action on each element spliterator() → returns a Spliterator for advanced/parallel traversal
Interface used to traverse elements Obtained through Iterable.iterator() Keeps track of the current position during iteration hasNext() → checks if another element exists next() → returns the next element remove() → removes the current element forEachRemaining() → processes remaining elements Iterator<String> it = names.iterator(); while (it.hasNext()) { String name = it.next(); } Iterable → can be iterated Iterator → performs the iteration Iterable.iterator() → gets an Iterator Iterable ↓ iterator() Iterator ↓ hasNext() / next() Elements Collection extends Iterable Therefore, List, Set, and Queue can be used with for-each Iterable ↓ Collection ├── List ├── Set └── Queue
Arrays Arrays can also be used with the enhanced for loop, but arrays do not implement Iterable.

main/localdate.html.title: LocalDate
main/localdate.html.description: Class representing a date without a time Stores year, month, and day Immutable and Thread Safe Part of the modern Java date/time API Useful when time of day and time zone are not needed LocalDate date = LocalDate.now(); System.out.println(date); LocalDate date = LocalDate.of(2026, 9, 9); now() → returns the current date of(year, month, day) → creates a date from its components parse(text) → creates a date from an ISO-8601 string LocalDate date = LocalDate.parse("2026-09-09"); getYear() → returns the year getMonth() → returns the Month getMonthValue() → returns the month as a number getDayOfMonth() → returns the day of the month getDayOfWeek() → returns the DayOfWeek getDayOfYear() → returns the day of the year lengthOfMonth() → returns the number of days in the month isLeapYear() → checks if the year is a leap year LocalDate is immutable, so methods that modify a date return a new LocalDate. LocalDate date = LocalDate.of(2026, 9, 9); LocalDate nextWeek = date.plusWeeks(1); LocalDate previousMonth = date.minusMonths(1); plusDays() / minusDays() → adds/subtracts days plusWeeks() / minusWeeks() → adds/subtracts weeks plusMonths() / minusMonths() → adds/subtracts months plusYears() / minusYears() → adds/subtracts years withYear() / withMonth() / withDayOfMonth() → changes a specific field LocalDate today = LocalDate.now(); LocalDate deadline = LocalDate.of(2026, 12, 31); if (today.isBefore(deadline)) { System.out.println("Before deadline"); } isBefore() → checks if a date comes before another isAfter() → checks if a date comes after another isEqual() → checks if two dates are equal equals() → compares the date values Note LocalDate does not contain a time or time zone. Use LocalDateTime when you need a time, or ZonedDateTime when you also need a time zone.

main/localdatetime.html.title: LocalDateTime
main/localdatetime.html.description:
Class representing a date and time without a time zone Combines LocalDate and LocalTime Stores year, month, day, hour, minute, second, and nanosecond
Immutable and Thread Safe LocalDateTime dateTime = LocalDateTime.now(); System.out.println(dateTime); LocalDateTime dateTime = LocalDateTime.of(2026, 9, 9, 14, 30); now() → returns the current date and time of() → creates a date and time from its fields parse(text) → creates a LocalDateTime from a string of(date, time) → combines a LocalDate and LocalTime LocalDate date = LocalDate.of(2026, 9, 9); LocalTime time = LocalTime.of(14, 30); LocalDateTime dateTime = LocalDateTime.of(date, time); getYear() → returns the year getMonth() → returns the Month getDayOfMonth() → returns the day of the month getHour() → returns the hour getMinute() → returns the minute getSecond() → returns the second toLocalDate() → extracts the LocalDate toLocalTime() → extracts the LocalTime Note LocalDateTime is immutable, so modification methods return a new object. LocalDateTime dateTime = LocalDateTime.of(2026, 9, 9, 14, 30); LocalDateTime later = dateTime.plusDays(2); LocalDateTime earlier = dateTime.minusHours(3); plusDays() / minusDays() → adds/subtracts days plusWeeks() / minusWeeks() → adds/subtracts weeks plusMonths() / minusMonths() → adds/subtracts months plusYears() / minusYears() → adds/subtracts years plusHours() / minusHours() → adds/subtracts hours plusMinutes() / minusMinutes() → adds/subtracts minutes LocalDateTime start = LocalDateTime.of(2026, 9, 9, 9, 0); LocalDateTime end = LocalDateTime.of(2026, 9, 9, 17, 0); start.isBefore(end); // true isBefore() → checks if it occurs before another date/time isAfter() → checks if it occurs after another date/time equals() → checks if two date/time values are equal
Note LocalDateTime does not contain a time zone or UTC offset. Use ZonedDateTime when the time zone matters, or Instant when you need a specific point in time.

main/localtime.html.title: LocalTime
main/localtime.html.description:
Class representing a time without a date Located in java.time Stores hour, minute, second, and nanosecond Immutable and Thread Safe Part of the modern Java date/time API Useful when a date and time zone are not needed LocalTime time = LocalTime.now(); System.out.println(time); LocalTime time = LocalTime.of(14, 30); now() → returns the current time of(hour, minute) → creates a time from hour and minute parse(text) → creates a time from an ISO-8601 string LocalTime time = LocalTime.parse("14:30:00"); getHour() → returns the hour getMinute() → returns the minute getSecond() → returns the second getNano() → returns the nanosecond toSecondOfDay() → returns the time as seconds since midnight toNanoOfDay() → returns the time as nanoseconds since midnight LocalTime is immutable, so methods that modify a time return a new LocalTime.LocalTime time = LocalTime.of(14, 30); LocalTime later = time.plusHours(2); LocalTime earlier = time.minusMinutes(15); plusHours() / minusHours() → adds/subtracts hours plusMinutes() / minusMinutes() → adds/subtracts minutes plusSeconds() / minusSeconds() → adds/subtracts seconds plusNanos() / minusNanos() → adds/subtracts nanoseconds withHour() / withMinute() / withSecond() → changes a specific field LocalTime start = LocalTime.of(9, 0); LocalTime end = LocalTime.of(17, 0); if (start.isBefore(end)) { System.out.println("Start is before end"); } isBefore() → checks if a time comes before another isAfter() → checks if a time comes after another equals() → checks if two times are equal
Note LocalTime does not contain a date or time zone. Use LocalDate for dates, or LocalDateTime when you need both a date and a time.

main/mathcontext.html.title: MathContext
main/mathcontext.html.description:
Class that defines the precision and rounding rules for BigDecimal calculations Controls how many significant digits are retained
Immutable MathContext mc = new MathContext(5); 5 → precision of 5 significant digits MathContext mc = new MathContext(5, RoundingMode.HALF_UP);
Defines both precision and rounding mode BigDecimal result = new BigDecimal("10") .divide(new BigDecimal("3"), mc); Applies the MathContext during the operation getPrecision() → returns the precision getRoundingMode() → returns the rounding mode MathContext.DECIMAL32 MathContext.UNLIMITED

main/period.html.title: Period
main/period.html.description:
Class representing an amount of date-based time Stores amounts in years, months, and days Commonly used with LocalDate
Immutable and Thread Safe Does not represent a specific date or time Period period = Period.ofDays(10); of(years, months, days) → creates a period from years, months, and days ofYears(years) → creates a period containing years ofMonths(months) → creates a period containing months ofWeeks(weeks) → creates a period containing weeks ofDays(days) → creates a period containing days between(start, end) → calculates the period between two dates parse(text) → creates a period from an ISO-8601 string Period period = Period.of(1, 2, 10); Represents:1 year + 2 months + 10 days getYears() → returns the number of years getMonths() → returns the number of months getDays() → returns the number of days getUnits() → returns the units used by the period isZero() → checks if the period has no amount isNegative() → checks if the period is negative plus() / minus() → adds or subtracts another period multipliedBy() → multiplies the period by a number negated() → returns the negative of the period normalized() → converts excess months into years A Period can be added to or subtracted from a date.LocalDate date = LocalDate.of(2026, 9, 9); LocalDate future = date.plus(Period.ofMonths(3)); LocalDate past = date.minus(Period.ofDays(10)); LocalDate start = LocalDate.of(2026, 1, 1); LocalDate end = LocalDate.of(2027, 3, 15); Period period = Period.between(start, end); period.getYears(); // 1 period.getMonths(); // 2 period.getDays(); // 14 Period → date-based amount: years, months, days Duration → time-based amount: hours, minutes, seconds, nanoseconds

main/printwriter.html.title: PrintWriter
main/printwriter.html.description: Class used to write formatted character/text output Provides convenient methods for writing text, numbers, and objects Commonly used with files, console output, and other character streams PrintWriter out = new PrintWriter("data.txt"); Creates the file if it doesn't exist Overwrites existing contents by default PrintWriter out = new PrintWriter( new FileWriter("data.txt", Charset.forName("utf8"), true) ); print() → writes a value without a newline println() → writes a value followed by a newline printf() → writes formatted output format() → writes formatted output write() → writes characters flush() → forces pending output to be written close() → closes the writer Note PrintWriter does not throw IOException from its print, println, or printf methods. Use checkError() to check whether an error occurred or pass in FileWriter.

main/properties.html.title: Properties
main/properties.html.description:
Class used to store key-value pairs of String values
Extends Hashtable<Object, Object>
Located in java.util
Commonly used for configuration settings
Often used with .properties files
Properties properties = new Properties(); properties.setProperty("username", "admin");
properties.setProperty("theme", "dark"); String theme = properties.getProperty("theme"); setProperty(key, value) → sets a property as a String key-value pair
getProperty(key) → returns the value associated with a key
getProperty(key, defaultValue) → returns a default value if the key doesn't exist
remove(key) → removes a property
containsKey(key) → checks if a key exists
containsValue(value) → checks if a value exists
stringPropertyNames() → returns all property names as a Set<String>
propertyNames() → returns an enumeration of all property names Properties can be loaded from a file or other input source.
Properties properties = new Properties(); try (FileReader reader = new FileReader("config.properties")) { properties.load(reader);
}
Example config.properties:username=admin
theme=dark
language=en
Then:String username = properties.getProperty("username"); Properties can be written to a file using store().
try (FileWriter writer = new FileWriter("config.properties")) { properties.store(writer, "Application Settings");
}
This produces a .properties file containing the key-value pairs.
load() → loads properties from an input stream or reader
store() → saves properties to an output stream or writer
loadFromXML() → loads properties from an XML file
storeToXML() → saves properties as XML
Note
Prefer setProperty() and getProperty() when working with Properties instead of the inherited put() and get() methods, because Properties is intended to work with String key-value pairs.

main/rounding-mode.html.title: Rounding Mode
main/rounding-mode.html.description:
enum that defines how rounding is performed Used by BigDecimal and MathContext Defines 8 rounding modes UP → rounds away from zero DOWN → rounds toward zero CEILING → rounds toward positive infinity FLOOR → rounds toward negative infinity HALF_UP → rounds to nearest; ties up HALF_DOWN → rounds to nearest; ties down HALF_EVEN → rounds to nearest; ties toward the even digit UNNECESSARY → rounding is not allowed; throws an exception if needed
Note RoundingMode defines how to round, while MathContext combines precision + rounding mode.

main/scanner.html.title: Scanner
main/scanner.html.description:
Accepts I/O classes on initialization Scanner sc = new Scanner(new File("io.txt"));
Scanner sc = new Scanner(System.in);
Scanner sc = new Scanner(str); Popular methods next()
nextLine()
nextInt()
nextLong()
nextDouble() Built-in type conversion
Invalid input results InputMismatchException
Prematurely closing the scanner object IllegalStateException

main/simpledateformat.html.title: SimpleDateFormat
main/simpledateformat.html.description:
Class for formatting and parsing dates/times using patterns Extends DateFormat Uses pattern letters to control the output format
Legacy API; prefer DateTimeFormatter for new code Not thread-safe SimpleDateFormat sdf = new SimpleDateFormat("yyyy-MM-dd"); String result = sdf.format(new Date()); System.out.println(result); // 2026-09-09 SimpleDateFormat sdf = new SimpleDateFormat("yyyy-MM-dd"); Date date = sdf.parse("2026-09-09"); format() → Date → String parse() → String → Date sdf.setTimeZone( TimeZone.getTimeZone("Asia/Manila") ); Controls the time zone used during formatting/parsing format() → formats a Date into a String parse() → parses a String into a Date applyPattern() → changes the pattern toPattern() → returns the current pattern setTimeZone() → sets the time zone setLenient() → controls handling of invalid dates
Note For modern Java, use DateTimeFormatter with java.time instead of SimpleDateFormat.

main/stringtokenizer.html.title: StringTokenizer
main/stringtokenizer.html.description: Class used to break a String into smaller parts called tokens Tokens are separated using delimiters Located in java.util Considered a legacy class; String.split() or Scanner are often preferred for newer code StringTokenizer st = new StringTokenizer("Hello World Java"); while (st.hasMoreTokens()) { System.out.println(st.nextToken()); } Output:Hello World Java StringTokenizer st = new StringTokenizer("Java is fun"); By default, whitespace characters are used as delimiters StringTokenizer st = new StringTokenizer("A-B-C", "-"); hasMoreTokens() → checks if more tokens are available nextToken() → returns the next token countTokens() → returns the number of remaining tokens hasMoreElements() → same as hasMoreTokens() nextElement() → same as nextToken(), but returns Object A delimiter determines where tokens are separated Multiple delimiters can be specified StringTokenizer st = new StringTokenizer("A,B;C", ",;"); , and ; are both treated as delimiters Note Delimiters are not included in the returned tokens by default. Initialization can be set to include them.

main/temporal.html.title: Temporal
main/temporal.html.description:
Package containing interfaces, classes, and fields used by the Java date/time API Provides a general way to access and manipulate date/time values Commonly used with LocalDate, LocalTime, and other java.time classes
Two important classes are ChronoField and ChronoUnit
Enum representing individual date/time fields Used to get or set specific parts of a temporal object Examples include year, month, day, hour, and minute LocalDate date = LocalDate.now(); int year = date.get(ChronoField.YEAR); int month = date.get(ChronoField.MONTH_OF_YEAR); YEAR → year MONTH_OF_YEAR → month DAY_OF_MONTH → day of the month DAY_OF_YEAR → day of the year DAY_OF_WEEK → day of the week HOUR_OF_DAY → hour of the day MINUTE_OF_HOUR → minute SECOND_OF_MINUTE → second NANO_OF_SECOND → nanosecond ChronoField ↓ Specific field ↓ YEAR / MONTH / DAY / HOUR / ...
Enum representing units of time Used when adding, subtracting, or measuring amounts of time Examples include days, weeks, months, years, hours, and minutes LocalDate date = LocalDate.now(); LocalDate future = date.plus(5, ChronoUnit.DAYS); NANOS → nanoseconds SECONDS → seconds MINUTES → minutes HOURS → hours DAYS → days WEEKS → weeks MONTHS → months YEARS → years DECADES → decades CENTURIES → centuries MILLENNIA → millennia ERAS → eras ChronoField → represents a field ChronoUnit → represents a unit of time ChronoField ChronoUnit YEAR YEARS MONTH MONTHS DAY DAYS HOUR HOURS MINUTE MINUTES LocalDate date = LocalDate.now(); date.get(ChronoField.YEAR); // get a field date.plus(5, ChronoUnit.DAYS); // use a unit Note What to use: ChronoField → "Which part?" ChronoUnit → "How much?"

main/timezone.html.title: Timezone
main/timezone.html.description:
Class representing a time zone and its time offset from UTC Used to determine how a date/time relates to a particular geographical time zone Commonly used with Calendar Handles time zone offsets and Daylight Saving Time (DST) rules
Modern Java generally prefers ZoneID and ZoneID > ZoneId and ZoneOffset TimeZone timezone = TimeZone.getDefault(); System.out.println(timezone.getID()); getDefault() → returns the system's default time zone getTimeZone(id) → returns a time zone for a given ID getID() → returns the time zone's ID setID(id) → changes the time zone's ID getOffset() → returns the offset from UTC getRawOffset() → returns the base offset from UTC, ignoring DST useDaylightTime() → checks if the time zone uses DST inDaylightTime(date) → checks if DST is active for a given date getAvailableIDs() → returns all available time zone IDs TimeZone timezone = TimeZone.getTimeZone("Asia/Manila"); getTimeZone() → obtains a TimeZone using its ID Common IDs:UTC Asia/Manila America/New_York Europe/London Asia/Tokyo TimeZone is commonly used to configure a Calendar.TimeZone timezone = TimeZone.getTimeZone("Asia/Manila"); Calendar calendar = Calendar.getInstance(timezone); The Calendar will now interpret its date/time using that time zone.int hour = calendar.get(Calendar.HOUR_OF_DAY); UTC offset → difference between a time zone's local time and UTC Example: UTC+08:00 means the local time is 8 hours ahead of UTC int offset = timezone.getRawOffset(); getRawOffset() returns the offset in milliseconds.UTC ↓ UTC+08:00 ↓ Local Time

main/zoneddatetime.html.title: ZonedDateTime
main/zoneddatetime.html.description:
Class representing a date and time with a time zone Combines LocalDateTime with a ZoneID Handles time-zone rules and UTC offsets Useful when the exact time zone matters
Immutable and thread-safe ZonedDateTime ├── LocalDate ├── LocalTime └── ZoneId ↓ Zone Rules ↓ ZoneOffset ZonedDateTime now = ZonedDateTime.now(); Uses the system's default time zone ZonedDateTime now = ZonedDateTime.now(ZoneId.of("Asia/Manila")); LocalDateTime dateTime = LocalDateTime.of(2026, 9, 9, 10, 30); ZonedDateTime zoned = dateTime.atZone(ZoneId.of("Asia/Manila")); now() → current date/time using the system zone now(ZoneId) → current date/time in a specific zone of(...) → creates a ZonedDateTime
getZone() → returns the ZoneID
getOffset() → returns the current ZoneOffset toLocalDate() → extracts the date toLocalTime() → extracts the time toLocalDateTime() → removes the zone information
withZoneSameInstant() → converts to another zone while keeping the same Instant plusDays(), plusHours() → adds time minusDays(), minusHours() → subtracts time isBefore(), isAfter() → compares date-times
For setting time zones, see ZoneID ZonedDateTime manila = ZonedDateTime.now( ZoneId.of("Asia/Manila") ); ZonedDateTime tokyo = manila.withZoneSameInstant( ZoneId.of("Asia/Tokyo") ); withZoneSameInstant() → same moment, different local time Manila 2026-09-09 10:00 +08:00 │ │ same instant ↓ Tokyo 2026-09-09 11:00 +09:00

main/zoneid.html.title: ZoneID
main/zoneid.html.description:
Class representing a time zone identifier Used with ZonedDateTime to represent a date and time in a specific time zone Uses IANA time zone IDs, such as Asia/Manila, Europe/London, and America/New_York Handles time-zone rules, including UTC offsets and daylight-saving changes
Immutable and thread-safe ZoneId zone = ZoneId.systemDefault(); ZoneId zone = ZoneId.of("Asia/Manila"); ZoneId zone = ZoneId.of("UTC"); systemDefault() → returns the system's default ZoneId of(String zoneId) → creates a ZoneId from an ID getId() → returns the time-zone ID getAvailableZoneIds() → returns all available time-zone IDs getRules() → returns the time-zone rules ZoneId zone = ZoneId.of("Asia/Manila"); ZonedDateTime dateTime = ZonedDateTime.now(zone); ZoneId → time-zone rules and region, e.g. Asia/Manila ZoneOffset → fixed offset from UTC, e.g. +08:00 ZoneId can have changing offsets because of daylight-saving rules ZoneId zone = ZoneId.of("America/New_York"); ZoneOffset offset = ZoneOffset.of("-04:00");
